summary: Describes how a pseudowire can carry PPP or HDLC units over an MPLS network without terminating the PPP/HDLC protocol. Service providers can offer emulated HDLC or PPP link services over existing MPLS networks. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A pseudowire lets a provider carry an old-style point-to-point link across a modern MPLS network. The packets travel inside MPLS labels, and the router at each end passes them on without ever running the link protocol itself.

questions: how does ppp over mpls work
what is the pseudowire control word
subtitle: Carrying PPP and HDLC links across an MPLS network as pseudowires, without ending the link protocol.

tldr.problem: Service providers want to offer emulated HDLC or PPP link services over their existing MPLS networks without terminating the PPP or HDLC protocol.
tldr.mechanism: A pseudowire carries each PPP or HDLC packet inside MPLS, behind a pseudowire label and an optional four-byte control word. HDLC drops the flags and the frame check sequence, and PPP also drops the HDLC framing.
tldr.outcome: The service is not a perfect emulation of a real PPP or HDLC link. Packet ordering needs the control word's sequence number, Frame Relay status messages are not processed, and some PPP options do not work if they are negotiated.

today: RFC 4618 is a Proposed Standard from September 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The pseudowire type codes it uses come from the registry defined in RFC 4446.

sections.title: Carrying PPP and HDLC Across an MPLS Network
sections.content:
A PPP/HDLC pseudowire allows PPP and HDLC protocol data units, the individual frames of those link protocols, to be carried over an MPLS network without terminating the PPP or HDLC protocol. The document assumes the pseudowire has been set up by some means outside its scope, either by manual configuration or with a signalling protocol such as the one in RFC 4447.

The reference model has a customer edge device at each end, connected to a provider edge router, with a packet-switched network between the two provider edge routers. PE1 is the ingress router and PE2 is the egress router. A layer 2 packet is received at PE1, encapsulated there, transported across the network, decapsulated at PE2, and transmitted out on an attachment circuit at PE2.

The pseudowire terminates at a logical port within the provider edge router. That port provides a native service processing function which delivers each PPP or HDLC packet it receives, unaltered, to the corresponding point in the provider edge router at the other end of the pseudowire. The native service processing function may include bit stuffing, bridging between pseudowires, layer 2 encapsulation, shaping and policing. These functions are specific to the native packet technology and may not be needed for the emulated service.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end of the link has a customer device and a provider router. The provider router wraps the link's frames in MPLS labels, sends them across the packet-switched core, and takes the labels off again at the far end. The frame itself passes through unchanged, and neither end router runs the PPP or HDLC protocol.

sections.title: What the Emulation Does and Does Not Do
sections.content:
PPP/HDLC transport over a pseudowire is not intended to emulate the traditional PPP or HDLC service perfectly, but it can be used for some applications that require PPP or HDLC transport service.

The differences from a real link are these. Packet ordering can be preserved using the optional sequence field in the control word, however implementations are not required to support this feature. The quality of service model for traditional PPP/HDLC links can be emulated, but that is outside the scope of this document. A Frame Relay port mode pseudowire, or an HDLC pseudowire, does not process any Frame Relay status messages or alarms. The HDLC flags are processed locally in the provider edge router connected to the attachment circuit.

The HDLC mode is suitable for port-to-port transport of Frame Relay user network interface or network node interface traffic. Since all packets are passed in a largely transparent manner over the HDLC pseudowire, any protocol that has HDLC-like framing may use it, including PPP, Frame Relay and X.25. Exceptions are cases where direct access to the HDLC interface is required, or modes that operate on the flags, the frame check sequence, or the bit and byte unstuffing that is performed before the HDLC packet is sent over the pseudowire. PPP asynchronous-control-character-map negotiation is an example of such a mode.

For PPP, because media-specific framing is not carried, three options will not operate correctly if the PPP peers attempt to negotiate them: frame check sequence alternatives, address-and-control-field compression, and asynchronous-control-character-map. PW LSP interface MTU negotiation is not affected by PPP maximum receive unit advertisement, so if a PPP peer sends a packet longer than the size negotiated for the pseudowire tunnel, that packet is discarded by the ingress router.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an emulation, not the real thing. Frame ordering only holds if the control word is used and carries a sequence number, and no implementation has to support that. Frame Relay alarms are ignored, and HDLC flags are handled by the router at each end rather than travelling. For PPP, three options cannot work: the frame check sequence alternatives, address-and-control-field compression, and the asynchronous control character map.

sections.title: The General Encapsulation Format
sections.content:
The general encapsulation format has four parts stacked on top of each other. The PSN transport header depends on the tunnelling technology in use and carries the encapsulated information through the packet-switched core. The pseudowire header identifies a particular PPP or HDLC service on a tunnel; in the case of MPLS it is the MPLS label at the bottom of the MPLS label stack. The control word is inserted before the PPP or HDLC service payload and may contain a length and a sequence number. Below that sits the PPP or HDLC service payload itself.

To use an MPLS label as the demultiplexer field, a 32-bit label stack entry is simply prepended to the emulated pseudowire encapsulation, so that it appears as the bottom label of an MPLS label stack. This label may be called the PW label. The particular emulated pseudowire identified by a particular label value must be agreed by the ingress and egress label switching routers, either by signalling or by configuration.

If quality of service information is to be carried, it should be represented in the EXP field of the PW label, and if the ingress router imposes more than one MPLS label, the EXP field of any labels higher in the stack must carry the same value. The ingress router must set the S bit of the PW label to 1, to denote that the PW label is at the bottom of the stack.
sections.plainLanguage: The encapsulated packet has up to four layers: whatever the tunnelling technology needs, the MPLS label that says which pseudowire this is, an optional control word, and the original link frame. The label goes at the bottom of the label stack and its bottom-of-stack bit is set to one.

sections.title: The Control Word
sections.content:
Four requirements may need to be satisfied when transporting layer 2 protocols over an MPLS network: sequentiality may need to be preserved, small packets may need to be padded so they can travel on a medium whose minimum transport unit is larger than the packet, control bits carried in the header of the layer 2 packet may need to be transported, and an in-band associated channel may be needed for operation and maintenance communications.

The control word is based on the generic pseudowire MPLS control word defined in RFC 4385. It provides the ability to sequence individual packets on the pseudowire and to avoid equal-cost multiple-path load-balancing, and it enables operation and management mechanisms. That last point matters because equal-cost multiple-path implementations may examine the first nibble after the MPLS label stack to decide whether the content is IP. If the PPP protocol number of a packet carried without a control word begins with 0x4 or 0x6, it could be mistaken for an IPv4 or IPv6 packet, which may lead to the packets of one pseudowire not following the same path.

The control word is 32 bits long. The first four bits are set to zero to indicate a control word. The next four bits carry protocol-specific flags, which are not used for HDLC or PPP and must be set to zero when transmitting and ignored on receipt. The next two bits are defined in RFC 4623. The next six bits are a length field: if the packet length, defined as the layer 2 payload plus the control word, is less than 64 bytes, the field must be set to the packet length, and otherwise it must be set to zero. A non-zero value is used to remove any padding added by the MPLS network, and that padding must be removed at the egress router before the packet is forwarded.

The last 16 bits are a sequence number that can be used to guarantee ordered packet delivery, although processing it is optional. The sequence number space is a 16-bit unsigned circular space, and the value 0 indicates an unsequenced packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The control word is four bytes in front of the payload. Its first bytes are fixed flags, then a six-bit length field that tells the far end how much padding the network added, and a two-byte sequence number that can be used to put the packets back in order. The control word itself is optional, but both ends must know whether the other one sends it.

sections.title: MTU Requirements
sections.content:
The network must be configured with an MTU that is sufficient to transport the largest encapsulation packets. When MPLS is used as the tunnelling protocol, for example, this is likely to be 12 or more bytes greater than the largest packet size. The methodology described in RFC 4623 may be used to fragment encapsulated packets that exceed the PSN MTU. However, if that document is not used, then if the ingress router determines that an encapsulated layer 2 packet exceeds the MTU of the tunnel through which it must be sent, the packet must be dropped.

If a packet is received on the attachment circuit that exceeds the interface MTU value signalled for the pseudowire, it must be dropped. It is also recommended that PPP devices be configured not to negotiate PPP maximum receive units larger than the MTU of the attachment circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: The network has to be able to carry the largest encapsulated packet, which is a little larger than the original frame. If a frame is still too big, it can be split using the method in RFC 4623, or it is dropped. A frame that is too big for the attachment circuit is always dropped.

sections.title: Protocol-Specific Details
sections.content:
HDLC. The HDLC mode provides port-to-port transport of HDLC-encapsulated traffic. The HDLC packet is transported in its entirety, including the HDLC address and control fields, but excluding the HDLC flags and the frame check sequence, and the bit and byte stuffing is undone. If the optional control word is used, the flag bits in the control word are not used and must be set to zero when transmitting and ignored on receipt. When the provider edge router detects a status change on the attachment circuit, such as a physical link failure or an administratively disabled circuit, it must send the appropriate pseudowire status notification message. The pseudowire of type 0x0006 carries HDLC packets.

Frame Relay port mode. This is an optional capability, also known as many-to-one mapping. Between two ports of Frame Relay devices, a number of Frame Relay virtual circuits are configured. Replacing that physical interface with a pair of provider edge routers and a pseudowire between them maps all of the virtual circuits carried over the interface into one HDLC pseudowire, while the standard Frame Relay link management interface procedures still happen directly between the customer edge devices. The virtual circuits are not visible individually to a provider edge router, which processes the set assigned to a port as an aggregate. This mode shares the HDLC encapsulation but uses a different pseudowire type, 0x000F for Frame Relay port mode; all other aspects are identical to the HDLC pseudowire.

PPP. The PPP mode provides point-to-point transport of PPP-encapsulated traffic. The PPP packet is transported in its entirety, including the protocol field whether or not it is compressed using protocol field compression, but excluding any media-specific framing information such as the HDLC address and control fields or the frame check sequence. PPP negotiation status is transparent to the pseudowire and must not be communicated to the remote provider edge router. The pseudowire of type 0x0007 carries PPP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: HDLC mode carries the whole frame apart from the flags and the frame check sequence, and it undoes the bit stuffing before sending. PPP mode also drops the HDLC address and control fields. Frame Relay port mode bundles all the virtual circuits of one port into a single pseudowire, and the routers treat them as one lump rather than looking at each circuit.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
The packet-switched network carrying the pseudowire may be subject to congestion, and during congestion it may exhibit packet loss that impacts the service carried by the pseudowire. Because PPP/HDLC pseudowires carry an unspecified type of service across the network, they cannot behave in the TCP-friendly manner prescribed by RFC 2914. In the presence of services that reduce their transmission rate, PPP/HDLC pseudowires will thus consume more than their fair share and should be halted.

Whenever possible, PPP/HDLC pseudowires should be run over traffic-engineered networks that provide bandwidth allocation and admission control. IntServ-enabled domains providing the Guaranteed Service, or DiffServ-enabled domains using expedited forwarding, are examples of such networks. The provider edge routers should monitor for congestion, using explicit congestion notification or by measuring packet loss, so that the service using the pseudowire may be maintained. When significant congestion is detected, the pseudowire should be administratively disabled. If the pseudowire was set up using the protocol in RFC 4447, the status notification procedures in that document can be used to stop packet transmission on the ingress router from the egress router. The pseudowire may then be restarted by manual intervention, or by automatic means after an appropriate waiting time.
sections.plainLanguage: When the core network is busy it drops packets, and this kind of traffic has no way to slow itself down politely, so it should be turned off. The provider edge routers are told to watch for congestion and disable the pseudowire when it is bad enough, and to run the pseudowire over a network that has reserved bandwidth where possible.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The PPP and HDLC pseudowire type is subject to all the general security considerations discussed in RFC 3985 and RFC 4447. This document specifies only encapsulations, and not the protocols that may be used to carry the encapsulated packets across the MPLS network. Each such protocol may have its own set of security issues, but those issues are not affected by the encapsulations specified here.
sections.plainLanguage: This document only defines how the frames are wrapped. Whether the traffic is protected depends on the protocol used to carry it across the network, and each protocol has its own security rules.
